title: Status Page Transparency Upgrades — Exec Update (Draft Slides)
content:
Slide 1 — Title
Status Page Transparency Upgrades
Reliability Program: Customer-Facing Incident Comms + Status Page Accuracy
Owner: Talia Benson (Program), SRE Sponsor: Sean Gallagher

Speaker notes:
Goal today: align on what’s changing, timeline, and where we need leadership support (policy + cross-functional adoption).


Slide 2 — Why this matters (customer + revenue)
Problem: the status page is not actionable enough during partial degradations
- Customers see “API Degraded” but can’t tell: streaming vs non-streaming, embeddings vs chat, which region, which model family
- Support/CS gets flooded with “what’s impacted?” and “should we fail over?” questions
- Enterprise expectations are rising (SLAs + security reviews increasingly ask for comms cadence + post-incident summaries)

What customers want
- Component-level clarity + region specificity
- Predictable update cadence with “next update by” time
- A short post-incident summary that matches internal reality without leaking sensitive details

Speaker notes:
This is about reliability outcomes and trust: faster understanding reduces customer churn risk and shortens customer-side mitigation time.


Slide 3 — Current pain signals (examples)
Recurring confusion themes (last ~60–90 days)
- Streaming-only incidents misrepresented as “API degraded” (SUP-18421)
- Region ambiguity: customers can’t tell whether to pin or fail over (SUP-18502)
- Enterprises requesting a timeline + written summary after partial outages (SUP-18455)

Observed internal friction
- Oncall spends time rewriting updates ad hoc
- Updates get delayed because we’re unsure what we can safely say
- Component selection inconsistent across teams/services

Speaker notes:
These are not “we need a prettier status page” requests. They’re operational and customer-impacting.


Slide 4 — Project goal (what ‘good’ looks like)
By end of rollout:
- Customers can quickly answer:
  1) What’s impacted? (specific product surface)
  2) Where? (region / deployment mode)
  3) What can I do right now? (workarounds / mitigation)
  4) When will I hear next? (timestamp)
- Internally:
  - Oncall can publish a high-quality update in minutes (template + prompts)
  - Status page stays in sync with incident state transitions (automation + guardrails)
  - Post-incident summaries are consistent and on-time for Sev1+ (SLA)

Speaker notes:
We’re reducing ambiguity. We are not overpromising root cause details; we’re standardizing clarity.


Slide 5 — Scope (what we are changing)
1) Component granularity (status page taxonomy)
Proposed customer-facing components (high level)
- API Gateway (request acceptance, auth, rate limits)
- Text/Chat Generation (non-streaming)
- Streaming (streaming transport + stream reliability)
- Embeddings
- Rerank
- Console
- Dedicated Control Plane
- Private Control Plane
- Region-specific Serving (Hosted API: us-east / us-west / eu-west)

2) Incident comms templates
- Copy-ready templates for: Investigating / Identified / Monitoring / Resolved
- Guidance: uncertainty language, customer actions, and next update time

3) Post-incident summaries
- Lightweight public summary aligned to internal postmortem categories
- Publication SLA: within 3 business days for Sev1/Sev0 (unless Security/Legal hold)

4) Tooling
- Incident-bot prompts + guardrails + draft-sync to status page

Speaker notes:
This is a cross-functional comms + reliability workflow upgrade; it doesn’t change our severity model or core incident roles.


Slide 6 — Out of scope (explicitly)
Non-goals
- Changing fundamental incident process (roles/severity definitions) beyond what’s needed for external comms
- Publishing sensitive details:
  - customer names / identifiable impacts
  - vulnerability-like exploitation details
  - confidential provider/partner contractual constraints
- Rebuilding the status page vendor/platform (we’ll work within current tooling constraints for this phase)

Speaker notes:
The point is consistent clarity, not over-disclosure.


Slide 7 — Plan + timeline (6–8 weeks)
Phase 1: Discovery (Weeks 1–2)
- Audit recent incidents + support tickets; identify top confusion drivers
- Finalize component taxonomy + mapping rules (internal signals → public components)
- Agree disclosure boundaries (Security/Compliance review)

Phase 2: Design (Weeks 2–3)
- Templates + cadence guidance
- Post-incident summary format + checklist
- Tooling design: incident-bot workflow + approvals

Phase 3: Implementation (Weeks 3–6)
- Add new components + region breakdown
- Incident-bot guided prompts; require next-update time entry
- Draft-sync from incident state transitions; human review before publish
- Summary workflow: auto-stub + reminders

Phase 4: Rollout (Weeks 6–8)
- Pilot in one region/service group
- Oncall training + enablement
- External announcement + updated public docs (“How to read our status page”)

Speaker notes:
Key is sequencing: taxonomy + templates first, then automation, then pilot + training.


Slide 8 — Early wins (already visible in pilot behaviors)
Qualitative wins (from oncall + Support feedback)
- Faster ‘time to first useful update’ when oncall uses phase templates
- Fewer back-and-forth messages to interpret impact (Streaming vs API confusion reduced in review threads)
- Better internal alignment on “what we can say” due to approval policy draft

Quant signals we’re tracking (initial baselines being finalized)
- Time-to-first-update (TTFU) for Sev1+: trending down in incidents where templates were used
- Support escalations during incidents: early downward signal in pilot group (Support notes)
- “Which component is affected?” follow-ups: fewer repeated questions in incident comms review threads

Speaker notes:
We’re careful on numbers today—baseline instrumentation is in progress—but directionally we’re seeing real reductions in comms friction.


Slide 9 — What we will measure (success metrics)
Customer-facing metrics
- Reduced incident-related support volume per incident (normalized by incident duration)
- Reduced enterprise escalations tied to unclear comms (CS renewal-risk notes)
- CSAT snippets during incident windows (where available)

Operational metrics
- Median time-to-first-status-update (Sev1+)
- % of updates that include: impact + mitigation + next update timestamp
- Update cadence compliance (by severity)
- Post-incident summary SLA compliance (Sev1/Sev0 within 3 business days)

Quality metrics
- Component selection accuracy (spot-audits vs internal signals)
- Consistency of impact language (classifier/helper adoption)

Speaker notes:
We care about speed + clarity, not just “more updates.” Guardrails prevent low-information updates.


Slide 10 — Key decisions / dependencies
Decisions needed
- Final approval workflow for external updates and summaries (who can publish; when to involve Security/Legal)
- Standard language commitments (avoid overpromising SLAs; align with Support macros)

Dependencies
- Status component mapping requires reliable signals per component (gap audit workstream)
- Incident-bot integration changes must be released safely (feature flags + canary)
- Docs updates must match policy and templates

Speaker notes:
The biggest risk isn’t engineering complexity; it’s adoption + consistency across teams.


Slide 11 — Risks + mitigations
Risk: Over-granularity confuses customers
- Mitigation: customer-friendly naming, definitions, and a public “How to read our status page” page

Risk: Slow updates due to approval bottlenecks
- Mitigation: pre-approved templates + clear escalation path when updates overdue

Risk: Under-disclosure (too vague) vs over-disclosure (security/privacy)
- Mitigation: disclosure checklist; Security/Compliance consult triggers; standardized “known/unknown” phrasing

Risk: Automation publishes incorrect info
- Mitigation: draft-sync (not auto-publish), human edit required, rollback plan/feature flag

Speaker notes:
We’re building guardrails both for speed and safety.


Slide 12 — What we need from leadership
1) Endorsement: make template usage mandatory for Sev1+ incidents (and recommended for Sev2)
2) Policy: confirm approvers and escalation path for external comms
3) Support alignment: approve standard customer guidance (retry/backoff, fallback models, region pinning) to reduce case load
4) Air cover for rollout: accept a short learning curve as we enforce higher update quality (guardrails)

Speaker notes:
This is a behavior change as much as a tooling change—leadership sponsorship is key.


Slide 13 — Appendix: Draft component taxonomy (1-pager)
Hosted API
- API Gateway
- Text/Chat Generation
- Streaming
- Embeddings
- Rerank
- Capacity & Routing (customer-facing label for scheduling/routing constraints; used when the symptom is 429/queueing/capacity)

Console
- Console

Dedicated
- Dedicated Control Plane

Private
- Private Control Plane

Regional overlays
- Hosted API Serving — us-east / us-west / eu-west

Speaker notes:
We’re intentionally avoiding internal terms like “scheduler” on the status page; “Capacity & Routing” was the leading customer-friendly option.


Slide 14 — Appendix: Template snippet examples (for exec visibility)
Investigating
- “We are investigating reports of elevated errors affecting Streaming in us-east. Non-streaming requests are not currently impacted. Next update by <time>.”

Identified
- “We identified an issue causing intermittent streaming disconnects. Mitigation in progress: <action>. Workaround: switch to non-streaming or retry with exponential backoff. Next update by <time>.”

Monitoring
- “Mitigation applied and metrics are improving. We are monitoring recovery. Next update by <time>.”

Resolved
- “This incident is resolved. If you continue to see issues, contact Support with request IDs. We will publish a post-incident summary within 3 business days.”

Speaker notes:
Core improvements: explicit scope, workaround, and next update time; plus consistency in phrasing.
